paragraphs: R' Yonatan ben Akhmai. (In Kaftor VaFerach, chapter 23, the reading is 'ben Agmai'.) Hyman calls him a disciple of R' Yohanan, citing [Sanhedrin 14a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.14a.7).[^1]

R' Yohanan regretted that Rav Shemen bar Abba was not there for them to ordain him. R' Shimon ben Zirud was with another sage. Who was the other? R' Yonatan ben Akhmai. They ordained the one who was there and did not ordain the one who was absent. Hyman takes the plain sense to mean that R' Yohanan ordained one of them.[^3]

And indeed, Hyman says, this is stated explicitly in the Yerushalmi, at [the end of Terumot](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Terumot.11.5.11) and in [Shabbat, chapter 2, end of halakhah 1](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Shabbat.2.1.20): Rabbi Abbahu said, 'Rabbi Yonatan ben Akhmai taught me' — Rabbi Zeira said to him, 'And what was his distinction?' He said to him, 'He is a great man and expert in our Mishnah, and Rabbi Hiyya of Kfar Tehumin made him known before Rabbi, and he appointed him sage.' (Hyman says it is known that all the Nesi'im are called in the Yerushalmi by the name Rabbi, or it is an abbreviation of רב״י, R' Yohanan.)[^2][^4]

notes.text: Hyman cites Kaftor VaFerach, chapter 23, for Agmai. The cited edition remains unverified.
The supplied Hebrew has פירשה with פירסם in parentheses. The latter supports “made him known.”

The Hebrew of the linked Sanhedrin reads Yonatan, while Davidson’s English gives Yochanan. The passage gives both orders of the pair and says “they ordained” one of them. Hyman takes Rabbi Yochanan to have ordained one. [Heilprin’s entry](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=1881&lang=en) records both the ordination and the Yerushalmi citation.

[Hyman’s printed p. 703](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/60/Aaron_Hyman._Toldoth_Tannaim_veAmoraim._II._1910.pdf#page=286) gives chapter 2 for Shabbat, where the supplied transcription has פ״ר. The Hebrew of the linked Shabbat titles Yonatan Rabbi and says “before Rabbi.” The parallel in Terumot leaves Yonatan untitled and says “before Rav.” Hyman considers “Rabbi” a title for a patriarch or an abbreviation for Rabbi Yochanan.
